title: Jonah's Great Fish
lead: "The LORD appointed a huge fish to swallow Jonah" (Jonah 1:17), and in the end "It vomited Jonah onto the dry land" (Jonah 2:10). The Hebrew says only "a great fish." The "whale" comes from the KJV's wording of Jesus' saying in Matthew 12:40. There the Greek word is ketos, a sea monster. Jesus made Jonah's three days in the fish the sign of his own death and rising.

sections.b: The narrator calls it dag gadol, "a great fish" (Jonah 1:17). Jonah himself never names it. Later in the same verse it is simply dag, "fish," and so it is when the LORD speaks to it (Jonah 2:10). In Jonah 2:1 the word is the feminine dagah. The book never says what kind of creature it was. The key verb is "appointed" (Hebrew vayman). God appoints the fish, then a plant, a worm and a hot east wind (Jonah 4:6–8). The sea, the fish, the plant and the worm all obey at once. Only the prophet runs. Inside the fish Jonah prays (Jonah 2:1): "From the belly of Sheol I cried for help" (Jonah 2:2). The fish is the place where he is as good as dead. It is also the means by which God saves him.

The Septuagint calls the great fish ketos mega, "a great sea creature" (Jonah 2:1 in its numbering). Matthew uses the same word in Jesus' saying: "Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster" (Matthew 12:40). The STEPBible Greek lexicon defines ketos as "a huge fish, sea-monster." It notes that the Greek Bible uses the same word for the great sea creatures of Genesis 1:21. The KJV turned it into "the whale's belly" in Matthew, but it kept "a great fish" in Jonah. The Latin Vulgate has piscem grandem, "a great fish." So "Jonah and the whale" is an English tradition, not the wording of the Hebrew or the Greek.

Jewish readers took the fish as real and full of wonder. Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer is a Jewish retelling of the Bible from the early Middle Ages (Sefaria dates it about 630 to 1030). In its chapter 10, Rabbi Tarfon says the fish was appointed from the six days of creation to swallow Jonah. Its two eyes were like windows of glass that gave Jonah light. Rabbi Meir adds that a pearl hung inside the fish and lit it like the noonday sun. The story goes on to have the fish show Jonah the depths of the sea and Leviathan. A comment printed under the name of Rashi (1040–1105) explains the feminine dagah of Jonah 2:1. Jonah had room in a male fish and did not pray. So God had him spat into a crowded female fish, and there he prayed. Sefaria's edition marks this comment as taken from Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer by way of the Yalkut Shimoni, and from Midrash Yonah.

Christian readers also took it as a miracle. When pagans laughed at the story, Augustine answered that anyone who believes Christ rose on the third day has no reason to doubt it. He also pointed to the huge ribs of a sea creature on public display in Carthage (Letter 102, AD 409). Jesus himself treats it as the sign for his generation: "Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster. In the same way the Son of Man will spend three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matthew 12:40). Other readers take the book of Jonah as a teaching story or parable. Then the fish belongs to the story's message rather than to a report of events. The chapter pages for Jonah 1 and Jonah 3 set out these readings. Either way, the fish serves the book's point: the LORD rules the sea and has mercy on whom he chooses, even a runaway prophet.
